l: the two-fold Fury, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The Fury is described as having an adamantine tread and as springing from a deep and dreadful ambush with many hands and hastening feet. It will visit Argive land to bring swift recompense.

l: Argive land, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Argive land is to be visited by the Fury as the place where swift recompense will be brought.

l: O chariot-course of Pelops, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The chariot-course of Pelops is addressed as full of toil, with an issue to the native soil that has been wearisome and sore.

l: Pelops, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Pelops is associated with the chariot-course that the Chorus describes as burdened by toil.

l: Pelopidae palace, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The house has continually accumulated crime and misfortune.

l: crime, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Crime is said to have mounted continually in the house of Pelops, beginning after Myrtilus was cruelly killed.

l: misfortune, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Misfortune is said to have mounted continually in the house of Pelops, alongside crime.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: Clytemnestra argues with Electra that the murder of Electra's father was justified because he sacrificed Clytemnestra's daughter at Aulis. An Old Man reports that Orestes died in a chariot accident at the Delphian games, and Clytemnestra rejoices that she is freed from fear of him and Electra. Electra is devastated by the report and believes she has lost her only hope of avenging her father. Clytemnestra takes the Old Man into the palace and leaves Electra outside to mourn.

l: Clytemnestra, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: Clytemnestra defends the murder of Electra's father, claiming that Justice killed him because he sacrificed her daughter. After hearing the Old Man's report that Orestes is dead, she rejoices that she is freed from fear of Orestes and Electra, though she admits that a mother cannot hate her child. She prays to Apollo for continued safety and prosperity and takes the Old Man into the palace.

l: Electra, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: Electra argues that Clytemnestra had no right to murder her father and condemns her for living with the blood-guilty Aegisthus. When the Old Man reports Orestes' death, Electra is devastated, believing that she has lost her only hope of avenging her father and her own suffering. She resolves to remain outside the palace and waste away among her enemies.

l: Orestes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: Orestes is reported to have won the foot-race at the Delphian games before entering a chariot race. He is said to have crashed after striking a stone, becoming entangled in the reins and being dragged by the horses until he died. His body was burned, and his ashes were placed in a bronze urn for burial in his homeland.

l: Aegisthus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: Aegisthus is away from home during the quarrel between Clytemnestra and Electra. His absence allows Electra to speak more freely, though Clytemnestra threatens that Electra will regret her boldness when Aegisthus returns.

l: Agamemnon, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: Electra's father sacrificed his daughter at Aulis so that the Greek fleet could sail to Troy, according to the account debated by Clytemnestra and Electra. Clytemnestra admits that she murdered him, while Electra argues that the sacrifice did not give Clytemnestra the right to kill him.

l: Clytemnestra's daughter, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: Clytemnestra's daughter was sacrificed by Electra's father at Aulis. Clytemnestra presents her death as the justification for murdering Electra's father, while Electra claims that he acted under painful constraint and not simply for Menelaus' sake.

l: Old Man, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: The Old Man arrives from Phanoteus the Phocian and reports that Orestes has died. He gives a detailed account of Orestes' victories, the chariot accident, the burning of his body, and the preparation of his ashes for burial. Clytemnestra accepts his report and brings him into the palace.

l: Chorus of Argive Women, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: The Chorus of Argive women observes the hostility between Clytemnestra and Electra and laments the reported destruction of the old royal line. It tries to comfort Electra after the report of Orestes' death, but Electra rejects its attempts to raise hope.

l: Justice, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: Clytemnestra claims that Justice, acting with her, killed Electra's father. Electra challenges this claim and warns that invoking such a precedent may bring repentance if Justice later judges Clytemnestra.

l: Delphi, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: Orestes is reported to have entered the chariot race at the Delphian games, described as a celebrated contest in Hellas. His earlier victory in the foot-race is also associated with this event.

l: Pelopidae palace, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: Clytemnestra prays to remain secure while ruling the Atridae's home and kingdom with the people she now lives with. She later enters the palace with the Old Man, leaving Electra outside.

l: sacrifice of Clytemnestra's daughter, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: The sacrifice took place at Aulis after Artemis stopped the winds because Electra's father had disturbed a sacred place and boasted after killing a deer. The sacrifice was presented as necessary for the Greek fleet to sail to Troy, though Electra says her father yielded only under painful constraint.

l: Agamemnon's murder, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: Clytemnestra admits that she murdered Electra's father and says the deed avenged the sacrifice of her daughter. Electra argues that the murder was driven instead by Clytemnestra's relationship with Aegisthus and was not authorized by any rightful law.

l: Orestes' chariot accident, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: During a chariot race, Orestes struck the edge of a stone after loosening the left-hand rein and shattered the axle. He fell, became caught in the reins, and was dragged by the horses until he died.

l: Orestes' death, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CLYTEMNESTRA.
s: The Old Man reports Orestes' death to Clytemnestra and Electra, saying that his body was burned and his ashes placed in a bronze urn. Clytemnestra welcomes the news as freedom from fear, while Electra mourns it as the destruction of her last hope.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: Chrysothemis believes that Orestes has returned after seeing offerings and a newly cut lock of hair at the ancient tomb of their father. Electra tells her that Orestes is dead and urges her to help kill Aegisthus, whom she identifies as the guilty author of their father's death. Chrysothemis refuses, arguing that they are women without sufficient strength and that such a plot would bring certain ruin. After their dispute, the Chorus praises filial piety, condemns the dishonor of the ancestral house, and honors Electra's loyalty and endurance.

l: Electra, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: Electra rejects Chrysothemis's belief that Orestes has returned and tells her that he is dead. She proposes that they kill Aegisthus to avenge their father's death, insisting that she will undertake the plan alone when Chrysothemis refuses.

l: Chrysothemis, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: Chrysothemis arrives joyfully, believing that Orestes has returned because she saw offerings and a newly cut lock of hair at the ancient tomb. She refuses Electra's proposal to kill Aegisthus, warning that their weakness and lack of support would make the attempt fatal.

l: Orestes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: Orestes is believed by Chrysothemis to have returned because of the offerings and lock of hair at the tomb. Electra states that he is dead and that salvation can no longer come from him.

l: Aegisthus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: Electra identifies Aegisthus as the guilty author of their father's death and proposes killing him. Chrysothemis says that Aegisthus is powerful and careful enough to prevent danger to himself.

l: Clytemnestra, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: Clytemnestra is referred to as the mother within the house. Electra argues that she would not have made the offerings at the tomb, and Chrysothemis says that the mother would have known if such an act had been performed.

l: Agamemnon, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: Agamemnon is referred to indirectly as the father and as the dead Atrides. The Chorus asks that a reproachful message be carried to dead Atrides and praises the loyalty shown toward the murdered father's memory.

l: the Chorus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: The Chorus praises birds for caring for those who raised them and warns that people who fail in similar filial duty will face divine recompense. It laments the division of the ancestral house, honors Electra's endurance and loyalty to divine law, and prays that she surpass her foes.

l: Agamemnon's tomb, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: The ancient tomb holds the sisters' father. Chrysothemis sees milk, garlands, and a newly cut lock of hair there, while Electra interprets the offerings as memorial gifts for Orestes.

l: Orestes' lock of hair, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: Chrysothemis finds a newly cut, youthful lock of hair beside the tomb and takes it as proof that Orestes has returned. Electra rejects this interpretation and says that the hair belongs among offerings made in memory of Orestes's death.

l: Orestes' death, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: Electra says that Orestes is dead and that she learned this from a man who witnessed his destruction. His death ends her hope that he will avenge their father's blood and leads her to seek Chrysothemis's help.

l: Agamemnon's murder, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: Electra refers to their father's death and seeks vengeance for the blood shed in it. She describes Aegisthus as the guilty author of the death and urges action against him.

l: the proposed killing of Aegisthus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: Electra proposes that she and Chrysothemis kill Aegisthus, believing that the act would honor their dead father and brother and restore their family's standing. Chrysothemis refuses to participate, fearing that the attempt would result in their destruction.

l: filial piety, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: The Chorus presents care for one's parents as a model of proper conduct, comparing human duty to the care birds provide for those who raised them. It praises Electra for remaining loyal to her father and for seeking to purge the family's shame.

l: prudence, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: Chrysothemis treats prudence and careful thought as the best protection in dangerous affairs. She uses prudence to justify submission to stronger enemies, while Electra views that caution as fear and refuses to follow it.

l: death, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ CHRYSOTHEMIS.
s: Electra says that death is not as hateful as being prevented from dying while desiring death. Chrysothemis warns that the proposed action could bring ruin and death, while the Chorus praises Electra's readiness to face death for vengeance and honor.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: Orestes and Pylades arrive at the palace carrying an urn and falsely report that Orestes has died in a chariot race. Electra mourns over the urn until Orestes reveals himself by his voice and Agamemnon's signet. The Old Man helps direct the plan, and Orestes and Pylades enter the palace, where Orestes kills Clytemnestra. Aegisthus then arrives, is deceived by the supposed corpse, recognizes Orestes, and is compelled to enter the palace to face death.

l: Orestes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: Orestes arrives with Pylades carrying an urn and pretends to be a Phocian messenger reporting his own death. He reveals himself to Electra through his voice and Agamemnon's signet, enters the palace, kills Clytemnestra, and confronts Aegisthus.

l: Electra, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: Electra receives the urn and mourns intensely, believing it contains Orestes' remains. She recognizes Orestes when he reveals himself, helps maintain the deception, urges him to kill Aegisthus, and remains outside to watch for his arrival.

l: Pylades, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: Pylades accompanies Orestes in the disguise involving the urn and enters the palace with him to carry out the planned revenge.

l: Clytemnestra, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: Clytemnestra believes the report that Orestes has died and prepares the urn for burial. She pleads for mercy when Orestes attacks her, but he kills her inside the palace.

l: Aegisthus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: Aegisthus rejoices at the report of Orestes' death and demands to see the supposed evidence. He discovers Clytemnestra's body and recognizes Orestes, then is forced into the palace to die in the place where Agamemnon was killed.

l: Old Man, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: The Old Man rebukes Orestes and Electra for delaying and warns them that their opportunity will be lost if they hesitate. He is revealed as the person who once conveyed Orestes secretly to Phocis and helped preserve him.

l: Chorus of Argive Women, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: The Chorus of Argive women reacts to Orestes' apparent death, his revelation, and the killings. It celebrates the progress of the avenger and declares that the curse has overtaken those responsible for earlier bloodshed.

l: Agamemnon, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: Agamemnon is identified as Orestes and Electra's father and as the man whose murder is to be avenged. Orestes and Aegisthus refer to the place where Agamemnon was killed.

l: Phocians, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: Orestes and Pylades pretend to be Phocians who have brought news of Orestes' death. Aegisthus asks where the Phocian men are and accepts their report as credible.

l: Pelopidae palace, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: The palace is the setting into which Orestes and Pylades enter to carry out their plan. Clytemnestra is killed inside it, and Aegisthus is ordered to enter it to meet his death.

l: brazen urn, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: The urn is presented as containing the remnants of Orestes' dead body. Electra receives it and mourns over it before learning that it contains only the false evidence used to deceive the household.

l: Orestes' signet, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: Orestes' signet, identified as belonging to Agamemnon, proves his identity to Electra. When he shows it, she recognizes him as her living brother.

l: Orestes' death, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: The death report falsely states that Orestes died in a chariot race and that his remains were brought in an urn. It deceives Clytemnestra and Aegisthus and allows Orestes to enter the palace safely.

l: Orestes's chariot race, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: The chariot race is the fabricated circumstance used to explain Orestes' supposed death. Aegisthus says he has heard that Orestes' life ended in such a race.

l: Agamemnon's murder, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: Agamemnon's murder is remembered as the crime for which Orestes seeks revenge. The place where Agamemnon was cut down is designated as the place where Aegisthus will die.

l: Clytemnestra's murder, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: Clytemnestra's murder is carried out by Orestes inside the palace after she pleads for mercy. Electra hears her cries and urges Orestes to strike again.

l: revenge against the murderers, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ORESTES _and_ PYLADES, _with the urn_.
s: The revenge against the murderers proceeds through the deception of the urn and the false death report. Orestes kills Clytemnestra and prepares to kill Aegisthus, while the Chorus declares that the guilty have been overtaken by the curse.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: Dêanira fears for Heracles, who has been absent for fifteen months, and recalls the prophetic scroll stating that he will either die after his campaign in Euboea or thereafter live free from trouble. Hyllus learns that Heracles is besieging Oechalia and agrees to seek news of him. Lichas arrives with captive women and reports that Heracles is alive and victorious, but a Messenger reveals that Heracles destroyed Oechalia because he loved Iole, its king's daughter, and has sent her to his household. Dêanira is shocked by the disclosure and confronts Lichas, who continues to deny or obscure the truth.

l: Deianira, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: Dêanira describes her fearful life as Heracles' wife, since he is repeatedly absent on labours and has now sent no word for fifteen months. She rejoices when told that Heracles is alive and victorious, but is distressed by the captive women and especially by the revelation that Iole has been brought into her household. She questions Lichas about Iole and learns that Heracles' campaign was motivated by love.

l: Heracles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: Heracles has been absent from Trachis for fifteen months while campaigning in Euboea. He has conquered Oechalia, taken its women captive, and sent Iole ahead to his household. According to the Messenger, he destroyed Oechalia because he loved Iole.

l: Hyllus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: Hyllus tells Dêanira that Heracles is said to have been enslaved to a Lydian girl and is now besieging Oechalia in Euboea. After hearing the prophecy concerning Heracles' fate, he agrees to go and investigate his father's situation.

l: the Chorus of Trachinian Maidens, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: The Chorus comforts Dêanira by urging her not to abandon hope and by affirming that joy and sorrow alternate in mortal life. It celebrates the report of Heracles' victory, but later recognizes the danger in Lichas's concealment of the truth.

l: the Messenger, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: The Messenger first tells Dêanira that Heracles is alive, victorious, and returning. He then stops her from taking the captive women inside, exposes Lichas's misleading account, and states that Heracles attacked Oechalia because of his love for Iole. He identifies the captive woman as Iole, daughter of Eurytus.

l: Lichas, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: Lichas arrives with captive women and tells Dêanira that Heracles is alive, healthy, and sacrificing in Euboea after conquering Oechalia. He presents the women as captives taken for the service of the gods and Heracles' household, but conceals or denies Iole's identity and the role of Heracles' love in the conquest. When confronted, he continues to give evasive answers.

l: Iole, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: Iole is brought to Trachis among the captive women after the fall of Oechalia. The Messenger identifies her as Iole, daughter of Eurytus, and says that Heracles conquered her father's city because he loved her. She does not speak in this unit.

l: Trachis, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: Trachis is the place where Dêanira and Heracles have been living in exile and where the action occurs. Heracles's household there receives the captive women, including Iole, after the conquest of Oechalia.

l: Euboea, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: Euboea is the region where Heracles is reported to be besieging or conquering Oechalia. Lichas says that Heracles is at a promontory of Euboea, sacrificing to Cenaean Zeus after his victory.

l: Oechalia, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: Oechalia is the city ruled by Eurytus that Heracles attacks and conquers. The Messenger says that its destruction was caused by Heracles' desire for Iole, Eurytus's daughter.

l: the robe, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: The introductory account states that Dêanira later commissions Lichas to present Heracles with a robe anointed with the blood-charm of Nessus, hoping to regain his affection. The robe is not yet presented or used in the dramatic action of this unit.

l: the prophetic scroll, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: Heracles left Dêanira an ancient scroll containing instructions about her marriage portion and the inheritance of their sons. It also set a time of fifteen months after his departure, after which Heracles would either die or live thereafter without trouble.

l: the captive women, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: The captive women are brought by Lichas to Trachis after Heracles's conquest of Oechalia. Dêanira pities them as formerly free women who have suddenly been reduced to captivity and orders that they be taken into the house.

l: the conquest of Oechalia, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: The conquest of Oechalia is described by Lichas as a victory for which Heracles is making sacrifices in Euboea. The Messenger gives a different account of its cause, saying that Heracles conquered the city because Eurytus would not yield Iole to him.

l: the death prophecy of Heracles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: The prophecy says that Heracles will either end his life after completing his undertaking in the land of Euboea or, if he survives the appointed time, enjoy a prosperous and trouble-free life. Dêanira connects this prophecy with the fifteen-month period recorded in the scroll.

l: the marriage of Dêanira and Heracles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: Dêanira recalls that Heracles won her in combat with the river-god Achelôüs and that she has since lived in continual fear because of his repeated absences. She describes herself as his wife and the mother of his sons, though Heracles spends little time at home.

l: the love of Heracles for Iole, The Seven Plays in English Verse, THE TRACHINIAN MAIDENS
s: The Messenger says that Heracles attacked and destroyed Oechalia because he loved Iole, the daughter of its king, Eurytus. Heracles then sent Iole to his household, where Dêanira receives her among the captives.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, DÊ. Nay, I entreat thee by His name, whose fire
s: DÊ asks Lichas to tell her the whole truth about Heracles and the maiden, saying that Love can overpower mortals and immortals alike. Lichas admits that the maiden's love for Heracles caused him to conquer Oechalia, and that he concealed this from DÊ out of concern for her feelings. DÊ resolves not to resist what she regards as the will of Heaven and orders Lichas to carry her message and gifts to the maiden.

l: Deianira, The Seven Plays in English Verse, DÊ. Nay, I entreat thee by His name, whose fire
s: DÊ urges Lichas to speak the truth about Heracles and the maiden, declaring that she will not blame either of them for a passion governed by Love. After learning the truth, she resolves to accept the situation rather than struggle against Heaven and prepares a message and gifts for the maiden.

l: Lichas, The Seven Plays in English Verse, DÊ. Nay, I entreat thee by His name, whose fire
s: Lichas confesses that the maiden's love for Heracles caused the conquest of Oechalia. He says that Heracles did not order him to conceal or deny this, but that he hid it because he feared wounding DÊ's heart.

l: Heracles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, DÊ. Nay, I entreat thee by His name, whose fire
s: Heracles is said to have been pierced by the maiden's love and wholly overmastered by it. He conquered Oechalia because of her love, and he did not command Lichas to conceal or deny the reason.

l: Iole, The Seven Plays in English Verse, DÊ. Nay, I entreat thee by His name, whose fire
s: The maiden's love for Heracles is identified as the sole cause of the conquest of Oechalia. DÊ pities her, believing that her beauty ruined her life and that she unknowingly ravaged and enslaved her own bright land.

l: Oechalia, The Seven Plays in English Verse, DÊ. Nay, I entreat thee by His name, whose fire
s: Oechalia is described as a land of plenteous woe that Heracles conquered with his spear because of the maiden's love for him.

l: Love, The Seven Plays in English Verse, DÊ. Nay, I entreat thee by His name, whose fire
s: Love is described as a force that leads even immortals at its will and cannot be successfully resisted. DÊ uses this power to explain why Heracles and others may be overcome by passion.

l: truth, The Seven Plays in English Verse, DÊ. Nay, I entreat thee by His name, whose fire
s: DÊ insists that Lichas reveal the whole truth, saying that the name of liar is hateful to a free-born person. Lichas then tells her that the maiden's love caused Heracles's conquest of Oechalia.

l: the conquest of Oechalia, The Seven Plays in English Verse, DÊ. Nay, I entreat thee by His name, whose fire
s: The conquest of Oechalia is attributed solely to the maiden's love for Heracles. Lichas says that Heracles did not ask him to conceal this cause, while DÊ accepts the event rather than adding to her misery by resisting Heaven.

l: gifts, The Seven Plays in English Verse, DÊ. Nay, I entreat thee by His name, whose fire
s: DÊ intends to send suitable gifts to the maiden in return for the gifts that have newly been given. She tells Lichas that he should not leave without carrying gifts from her.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Deianira gives Heracles a robe treated with the Centaur's gift, hoping to secure his love and prevent his attachment to the captive maiden. When the ointment causes wool exposed to sunlight to dissolve and foam, Deianira realizes that Nessus deceived her and that the gift may be poisonous. Hyllus reports that Heracles was afflicted by the robe during a sacrifice, killed Lichas in agony, and ordered that he be carried away. Hyllus condemns Deianira as his father's killer, and she silently leaves, resolving that her own death should follow if Heracles dies.

l: Deianira, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Deianira explains that she has brought the captive maiden into her household and fears that Heracles will make the younger woman his mate rather than remain devoted to her. She sends Heracles a robe treated with the Centaur's gift, then becomes terrified when the wool used to apply it dissolves in sunlight and concludes that she may have caused Heracles' death. After Hyllus reports Heracles' suffering and condemns her, Deianira leaves in silence.

l: Heracles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Heracles returns after sacking Eurytus' city and sends the captive maiden to his household. At Cenaeum, he wears Deianira's robe while sacrificing to Zeus, but the garment clings to his body and causes violent internal pain. He blames the gift, kills the guiltless Lichas in agony, and orders Hyllus to carry him away from the place.

l: Hyllus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Hyllus witnesses Heracles' poisoning and reports that the robe caused his father's convulsions, agony, and furious actions. He tells Deianira that she has killed Heracles and invokes Right and Vengeance against her, rejecting the claim that she has acted as a mother. He then leaves her.

l: Nessus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Nessus ferried travelers across the Evenus and, while carrying Deianira, touched her wantonly. Heracles killed him with an arrow, and while dying Nessus told Deianira to collect the blood from his wound as a charm to preserve Heracles' love. Deianira later realizes that Nessus deceived her in order to destroy Heracles.

l: the Chorus of Trachinian Maidens, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus first celebrates Heracles' expected return and recalls that Deianira has long suffered in fear and separation. It accepts Deianira's plan to use the Centaur's gift, though it notes that her confidence lacks proof. After the robe's destructive effect is revealed, it acknowledges her fear but says that an unwitting error lessens the basis for wrath.

l: the Centaur's blood, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The Centaur's gift is an ancient substance that Deianira kept hidden in a bronze urn and applied to Heracles' robe. Deianira believed it would prevent Heracles from receiving another love, but the substance instead destroys the wool exposed to sunlight and contributes to Heracles' suffering.

l: the ointment, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Deianira spreads the ointment over the robe with a tuft of wool, following the Centaur's instruction to keep it away from heat and sunlight. When the wool is exposed to Helios' beam, it crumbles away and leaves seething, foamy clots, revealing the ointment's destructive nature.

l: the robe, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Deianira sends the finewoven robe to Heracles with instructions that it not be worn before him or exposed to sun, temple, or household flame until he displays it during sacrifice. Heracles wears it at Cenaeum, where it becomes glued to his body and causes tearing pains and violent convulsions.

l: the arrow, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The arrow fired by Heracles at Nessus penetrates his chest and is described as having been dyed with the dark gall of a monster snake. Deianira later learns that the venom from the arrow's wound may ravage whatever it touches.

l: Lernaean Hydra's poison, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The poison comes from the gory venom of Nessus' wound and spreads blackly from the robe's effect. It burns or consumes Heracles' body, producing severe pain, convulsions, and agonized cries.

l: Heracles' poisoning, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Heracles is poisoned when he wears Deianira's treated robe during sacrifice at Cenaeum. The garment clings to him as the poison attacks, and he suffers convulsions, screaming, and intense pain before ordering Hyllus to carry him away.

l: Deianira's guilt, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Deianira initially believes she has acted without criminal intent and only to preserve Heracles' affection. After the wool's destruction and Hyllus' report, she recognizes that Nessus deceived her and fears that she is Heracles' murderess.

l: jealousy and marital fidelity, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Deianira's jealousy arises from Heracles bringing home a younger captive woman whom she fears he will prefer as a mate. She attempts to preserve marital fidelity and Heracles' love through the robe, while acknowledging that a prudent wife should not openly resent such a rival.

l: death and vengeance, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Hyllus calls for Right and Vengeance to punish Deianira for causing Heracles' suffering and death. Deianira declares that if Heracles is harmed, her own death will follow, and Hyllus wishes that she would be swept away from his sight.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Deianira dies by stabbing herself after realizing that the robe she sent to Heracles has caused his torment, while Hyllus learns that she acted innocently under Nessus's deception. Heracles is brought in suffering terribly, condemns Deianira before learning of her death, and then understands that Nessus has fulfilled the prophecy of his own death. He orders Hyllus to carry him to Mount Oeta, build a pyre, and burn his body, and he also commands Hyllus to marry Iole. Hyllus reluctantly swears to obey, while the Chorus mourns the ruin brought upon Heracles's household.

l: Heracles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Heracles is brought in on a litter, suffering unbearable pain from the robe sent by Deianira. After learning that Deianira has died and acted under Nessus's deception, he interprets the prophecies as foretelling his death and commands Hyllus to burn him on Mount Oeta. He also orders Hyllus to marry Iole.

l: Hyllus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Hyllus brings and supports his suffering father, Heracles, and explains that Deianira acted innocently under Nessus's influence. He swears to carry Heracles to Mount Oeta and prepare the pyre, though he initially resists marrying Iole because he blames her for the disaster. He ultimately agrees to obey Heracles.

l: Deianira, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Deianira dies by her own hand after discovering that the robe she sent to Heracles has destroyed him. Before her suicide, she laments her abandonment and prepares the fatal blow; Hyllus later declares that she acted with good intentions and without knowing the robe's true effect.

l: Iole, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Iole is identified as the daughter of Eurytus and the maiden who came from Heracles's conquest of Oechalia. Heracles commands Hyllus to marry her after his death.

l: the Chorus of Trachinian Maidens, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus mourns Deianira's death, Heracles's suffering, and the ruin of his household. It fears the arrival of Heracles and laments the destruction brought about by divine and fated forces.

l: Nessus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Nessus is identified as the Centaur whose deceptive advice led Deianira to use the robe as a love charm. Though Nessus is dead, Heracles understands that Nessus has thereby caused his living death.

l: Zeus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Zeus is invoked as the supreme ruler and as Heracles's divine father. Heracles appeals to Zeus for relief from his torment and calls on him as witness when Hyllus swears to obey.

l: Trachis, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Trachis is the place where Heracles's household is located and where Deianira dies. Hyllus refers to Trachis when asking whether it contains a magician capable of producing the love charm.

l: Oeta, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Mount Oeta is the place where Heracles orders Hyllus to take his body. He directs Hyllus to build a pyre there from oak and wild olive wood and burn him with pine flame.

l: Lernaean Hydra's poison, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The poison associated with the Lernaean Hydra is described as the venom on the shaft that supplied the deadly substance used by Nessus. It contributes to the robe's destructive power against Heracles.

l: the robe, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Nessus's robe is the garment Deianira sends to Heracles as a supposed charm to restore his love. When Heracles wears it, it clings to his body, consumes his flesh, and causes the agonizing suffering that will lead to his death.

l: Heracles' funeral pyre, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The pyre is the structure Heracles commands Hyllus to build on Mount Oeta. Heracles intends it to consume his body and end his torment.

l: Heracles's death, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Heracles's death is presented as imminent and as the fulfillment of prophecies that his labors will end when he enters the new phase of life that follows them. He understands that Nessus, though dead, has caused this death, and he orders Hyllus to bring it about through the pyre.

l: Deianira's suicide, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Deianira's suicide occurs inside the household after she realizes that her gift has fatally harmed Heracles. She uses a blade against herself, and Hyllus recognizes too late that she acted from misguided love rather than deliberate malice.

l: Heracles's suffering, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Heracles suffers repeated convulsions and extreme pain as the robe eats through his flesh to the bone and damages his vital channels. He calls for death, asks Hyllus to kill him, and says that no previous labor or enemy caused comparable torment.

l: the death prophecy of Heracles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Heracles recalls a prophecy from his father that he would die through the will of someone already dwelling among the dead, which he identifies with the dead Nessus. He also recalls oracles from the sacred tree stating that his labors would end when a new period of life began, and he now understands this as a prophecy of death.

l: Heracles's funeral sacrifice, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Heracles orders Hyllus to perform the funeral act by carrying him to Mount Oeta, gathering wood, and setting the pyre alight. He requires Hyllus to do this without mourning tears, presenting the burning as the only release from his suffering.

l: Hyllus's marriage to Iole, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Heracles commands Hyllus to marry Iole after Heracles's death and not allow another man to take her. Hyllus objects because he connects Iole with the disaster, but he finally agrees to fulfill his father's command.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, PHILOCTETES
s: Odysseus brings Neoptolemus to the deserted shore of Lemnos to recover Philoctetes and the bow of Heracles, which prophecy says are necessary for Troy's capture. He instructs Neoptolemus to deceive Philoctetes by claiming hatred for the Achaean army and Odysseus, while Odysseus withdraws to avoid being recognized. Neoptolemus initially objects to lying but agrees to the plan after Odysseus argues that neither force nor persuasion can obtain the bow. The Chorus of Mariners joins Neoptolemus, and Philoctetes is heard approaching in great pain from his isolated dwelling.

l: Odysseus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, PHILOCTETES
s: Odysseus leads Neoptolemus to Lemnos to recover Philoctetes and his bow. He orders Neoptolemus to entrap Philoctetes through deceit, then withdraws so that Philoctetes will not recognize him, planning to return in disguise as a merchantman if necessary.

l: Neoptolemus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, PHILOCTETES
s: Neoptolemus searches Philoctetes' cave and reports its furnishings and signs of habitation. He objects to lying because it conflicts with his nature and sense of honor, but agrees to follow Odysseus' deceptive plan after learning that the bow is needed to take Troy.

l: Philoctetes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, PHILOCTETES
s: Philoctetes has been abandoned on Lemnos because his foot wound caused loud cries that disturbed the army's rites and sacrifices. He lives alone in a cave, obtains food by shooting wild creatures, and is heard approaching while crying out in severe pain.

l: Chorus of Mariners, The Seven Plays in English Verse, PHILOCTETES
s: The Chorus of Mariners enters after Odysseus withdraws and offers to support Neoptolemus' mission. It learns the location of Philoctetes' cave and expresses pity for his solitary life, disease, hunger, and suffering before hearing him draw near.

l: Lemnos, The Seven Plays in English Verse, PHILOCTETES
s: Lemnos is the deserted island where Philoctetes has been cast away. Its shore is described as uninhabited and untrodden by men.

l: Troy, The Seven Plays in English Verse, PHILOCTETES
s: Troy can be taken only through the combined aid of Neoptolemus and Philoctetes' bow. Odysseus says that Troy's destined fall depends on obtaining the bow and bringing Philoctetes back.

l: the bow of Heracles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, PHILOCTETES
s: The bow of Heracles is in Philoctetes' possession and is described as having arrows that cannot miss and bring death. Odysseus says that the bow alone has the power to take Troy, though it is also useless without Neoptolemus.

l: Philoctetes' wound, The Seven Plays in English Verse, PHILOCTETES
s: Philoctetes' wound is an ancient, festering injury in his foot that makes his movement difficult and causes severe pain. It led the army to reject and cast him away, and he has no healer to relieve it.

l: Helenus' prophecy, The Seven Plays in English Verse, PHILOCTETES
s: Prophecy reveals that Philoctetes must return with the bow for Troy to be taken. Neoptolemus says that the prophecy prevents Philoctetes from bending his deadly shaft against Troy before the destined time.

l: fate's decree, The Seven Plays in English Verse, PHILOCTETES
s: Fate's decree is that Troy must be taken by Neoptolemus, assisted by the bow of Heracles in Philoctetes' hands. This decree motivates Odysseus' attempt to bring Philoctetes back.

l: conquest of Troy, The Seven Plays in English Verse, PHILOCTETES
s: The capture of Troy depends on Neoptolemus and Philoctetes acting together with the bow. Odysseus says that Neoptolemus without the bow and the bow without Neoptolemus are both powerless.

l: Philoctetes' exile, The Seven Plays in English Verse, PHILOCTETES
s: Philoctetes was cast away by Odysseus on Lemnos after the army rejected him because his wound caused disruptive cries during rites and sacrifices. He has remained isolated from human companionship and care.

l: Philoctetes' cave, The Seven Plays in English Verse, PHILOCTETES
s: Philoctetes' cave has two openings, offering sunshine in winter and breezes in summer. Neoptolemus finds a bed of leaves, a wooden cup, fire embers, and festering rags used as dressings for a malignant sore.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Philoctetes tells Neoptolemus how the Atridae and Odysseus abandoned him on Lemnos with a grievous plague, leaving him to survive alone for ten years. Neoptolemus recounts how Odysseus and the Atridae deprived him of Achilles' armour, and he declares his hatred for them. A merchantman reports that Odysseus and Diomedes are pursuing Philoctetes because Helenus prophesied that Troy cannot be taken without him. Neoptolemus agrees to take Philoctetes home, but after learning of the pursuit, he and Philoctetes prepare to depart with Philoctetes' bow and other necessities.

l: Philoctetes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Philoctetes meets Neoptolemus and recounts his abandonment on Lemnos, his ten years of suffering, and the means by which he has survived. He begs Neoptolemus to take him home, and Neoptolemus agrees before the arrival of news that the Argives are pursuing him.

l: Neoptolemus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Neoptolemus identifies himself as Achilles' son from Scyros and tells Philoctetes how Odysseus and the Atridae wronged him over Achilles' armour. He agrees to carry Philoctetes home and prepares to depart with him.

l: Odysseus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Odysseus is described as a deceitful and harmful man who took Achilles' armour from Neoptolemus and helped abandon Philoctetes. He captures Helenus, learns the prophecy concerning Philoctetes, and sets out with Diomedes to bring Philoctetes back by persuasion or force.

l: Achilles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Achilles is identified as Neoptolemus' father and as a man whom Philoctetes knew and esteemed. He is reported to have died after being struck by Phoebus' shaft.

l: Atreidae, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: The Atreidae are blamed by Philoctetes and Neoptolemus for cruelly abandoning Philoctetes and for depriving Neoptolemus of Achilles' armour. They now seek Philoctetes because his presence is required for the capture of Troy.

l: Lemnos, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Lemnos is the deserted island where Philoctetes was left after the fleet touched there from Chrysa. It has no proper harbour or sea-port, and Philoctetes has lived there in isolation for ten years.

l: Scyros, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Scyros is Neoptolemus' native, sea-girt home. Neoptolemus says that he intends to return there and be content with his life at home.

l: Troy, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Troy is the city against which the Greeks sailed, and Neoptolemus initially joined the expedition because he was told that he alone could take its citadel. Helenus' prophecy states that Troy cannot be captured until Philoctetes is brought from Lemnos.

l: Philoctetes' cave, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Philoctetes' cave on the cliff by the shore has been his bare dwelling-place since the Greeks left him. He goes inside with Neoptolemus to collect the few things he cannot leave behind.

l: Philoctetes' wound, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Philoctetes' plague is a fierce and worsening malady caused by the bite of a murderous basilisk. It causes severe suffering, and a leaf kept in the cave can quiet its rage and lull it to rest.

l: the bow of Heracles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: The bow that descended from Heracles is Philoctetes' sole great possession and has enabled him to hunt birds for food. Neoptolemus asks to handle it, and Philoctetes permits him to take it temporarily.

l: Achilles' armour, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Achilles' armour was sought by Neoptolemus after Achilles' death, but the Atridae told him that Odysseus wielded it. Odysseus claimed that he had saved the armour and its former master, and Neoptolemus returned to Scyros deprived of his inheritance.

l: ship, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Neoptolemus' ship is intended to carry him and Philoctetes away from Lemnos toward home. A south-western head-wind delays their course, but Neoptolemus plans to sail when possible.

l: Philoctetes' exile, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: The two generals and Odysseus left Philoctetes on Lemnos after his basilisk wound became unbearable, providing only scant rags and food. He awoke to find the fleet gone and survived alone for ten years without human assistance.

l: the prize-encounter for Pelides' arms, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Neoptolemus calls the loss of Achilles' arms a robbery carried out when the Atridae gave them to Odysseus. He regards the Atridae as chiefly responsible, though he also condemns Odysseus for taking them.

l: Helenus' prophecy, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Helenus, a princely seer and son of Priam, prophesied that the Greeks could not sack Troy until they brought Philoctetes from Lemnos. Odysseus captured Helenus and used this prophecy to initiate the pursuit of Philoctetes.

l: the Argive pursuit of Philoctetes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Phoenix, Acamas, and Demophon are reported to be coming with ships and men to recover Philoctetes, while Odysseus and Diomedes are already pursuing him under oath. They intend to bring him to the Argive camp by reasons if possible and by force if necessary.

l: the Trojan War, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: The Trojan War brought Neoptolemus to Troy and led to the disputes over Achilles' death and armour. It also resulted in Philoctetes' abandonment and, according to Helenus' prophecy, cannot be successfully concluded without him.

l: Philoctetes' return home, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ PHILOCTETES.
s: Philoctetes hopes to return to Oeta, see his father, and reach the ridge of Trachis and the Spercheius. Neoptolemus promises to take him home, and the two prepare to leave Lemnos before Odysseus can seize him.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Philoctetes suffers a severe recurrence of his wound while Neoptolemus guards him and receives his bow. After Philoctetes sleeps, Neoptolemus reveals that he is expected to take Philoctetes to Troy so that the plague may be cured, and Philoctetes accuses him of betrayal and demands the bow back. Odysseus arrives, orders Philoctetes to be forced aboard, and claims that Zeus has decreed the voyage. Odysseus eventually releases Philoctetes, but Neoptolemus delays departure, still troubled by pity for him.

l: Philoctetes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Philoctetes suffers a violent attack of his wound, begs Neoptolemus not to abandon him, and entrusts him with the bow. When Neoptolemus reveals the plan to take him to Troy, Philoctetes denounces the betrayal, demands his bow, refuses to sail, and curses Odysseus and the Atreus' sons. Odysseus orders him bound, but later releases him when he decides the bow is sufficient.

l: Neoptolemus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Neoptolemus remains beside Philoctetes during the attack, guards the bow, and helps him after he sleeps. He tells Philoctetes that he is to sail to Troy and help take the realm, then suffers shame and distress over the deceit. Neoptolemus admits pity for Philoctetes and delays leaving when Odysseus orders the party to depart.

l: Odysseus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Odysseus arrives and orders Neoptolemus to surrender the bow and return, while commanding that Philoctetes be forced to sail. He claims that Zeus has willed the voyage and says that Philoctetes must join the attack on Troy. After Philoctetes resists, Odysseus orders him seized, then releases him because he believes the bow alone is sufficient.

l: Chorus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus describes Philoctetes' long isolation, hunger, wound, and suffering on the island. It urges sleep to bring him relief and repeatedly asks Neoptolemus to consider whether to stay or sail. Later, it leaves the decision to its captain while acknowledging Philoctetes' bitterness and Neoptolemus' pity.

l: Achaeans, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The Achaean host is the force to which Philoctetes is to be taken at Troy. Philoctetes says that its generals abandoned him and that the host would use his bow in the war.

l: Lemnos, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Lemnos is the island where Philoctetes has lived in abandonment and where he threatens to die rather than sail. Its earth, flame, rocks, creeks, precipices, and familiar presence are invoked by Philoctetes as witnesses to his suffering.

l: Troy, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Troy is the destination to which Neoptolemus is ordered to take Philoctetes. Philoctetes is told that he must join the chieftains and the Achaean host there, and Odysseus says that he is to help ravage Troy.

l: Philoctetes' cave, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Philoctetes' cave is the place where he has lived companionless and from which Neoptolemus leads him during the attempted departure. Philoctetes threatens to return to it, robbed of his arms and food, if he is left behind.

l: Philoctetes' wound, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Philoctetes' wound suddenly erupts in severe pain and bleeding, producing a gory flow and dark blood from his foot. It weakens him so completely that he collapses and requires sleep before he can recover.

l: Philoctetes' pain, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Philoctetes' pain is described as unutterable, soul-devouring, and capable of making him beg for death. During its recurrence he asks Neoptolemus to cut off his foot, burn him, or remain beside him until sleep relieves the attack.

l: the voyage to Troy, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The voyage to Troy is presented as commanded by heaven and necessary for Philoctetes to join the Achaean host. Philoctetes refuses it because of his suffering and past abandonment, while Odysseus seeks to force it and Neoptolemus hesitates.

l: the Trojan War, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The conflict at Troy is the setting for the Achaean host's need for Philoctetes and his bow. Philoctetes says that the generals abandoned him during the earlier expedition, while Odysseus says that Philoctetes must now help ravage Troy.

l: the bow of Heracles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: The bow, described as the sacred gift and reward of Zeus-born Heracles, is entrusted by Philoctetes to Neoptolemus during his attack. Neoptolemus uses deceit to retain it, and Odysseus ultimately decides that the bow can serve the Achaean cause without Philoctetes.

l: pity and mercy, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Neoptolemus repeatedly shows pity for Philoctetes' suffering and feels troubled by the wrong he has done him. His pity leads him to delay departure after Odysseus releases Philoctetes, although he has not yet restored the bow.

l: deceit and moral right, The Seven Plays in English Verse, CHORUS.
s: Deceit is used by Neoptolemus to obtain Philoctetes' bow under the appearance of friendship and protection. Philoctetes condemns this act as betrayal, and Neoptolemus recognizes it as a shameful deed learned from base men.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Philoctetes, abandoned on Lemnos because of his wound, mourns his suffering and refuses to sail to Troy or aid the Achaeans. Neoptolemus returns the bow he took by deceit, but Philoctetes still rejects the proposed voyage until Heracles appears and declares that Zeus requires Philoctetes and Neoptolemus to conquer Troy together. Heracles promises that Philoctetes will be healed by Asclepius and will win glory through the conquest of Troy. Philoctetes then bids farewell to Lemnos, and he and the Chorus prepare to sail for Troy.

l: Philoctetes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Philoctetes laments his isolation, hunger, wound, and exile in his cave on Lemnos. He initially curses the Achaeans and refuses to return to Troy, but after Heracles commands him, he agrees to sail with Neoptolemus, be healed, and help conquer Troy.

l: Neoptolemus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Neoptolemus repents of obtaining Philoctetes' bow through deceit and returns it to him despite Odysseus' opposition. He tries to persuade Philoctetes to sail to Troy, and Heracles declares that Neoptolemus and Philoctetes must conquer Troy together.

l: Odysseus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Odysseus opposes Neoptolemus' decision to return Philoctetes' bow and threatens to report him to the Achaean army. He appears again to assert that Philoctetes will be forced to go to Troy, but leaves when Philoctetes threatens him with the bow.

l: Heracles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Heracles appears from above as a divine messenger and tells Philoctetes and Neoptolemus what Zeus intends. He promises Philoctetes healing, glory, and victory at Troy, and instructs the two men to protect one another and honor the gods.

l: Chorus of Mariners, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: The Chorus first urges Philoctetes not to reject their friendship and tries to persuade him to go to Troy. After Heracles' appearance, it prepares to sail with Philoctetes and Neoptolemus and prays for the sea nymphs to protect their voyage.

l: Achaeans, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: The Achaean army is said to oppose Neoptolemus' return of Philoctetes' bow and would punish him for that act. Philoctetes continues to hate the army for abandoning him because of his wound.

l: Atreidae, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: The Atreidae are blamed by Philoctetes for casting him onto Lemnos and for destroying his life. He fears returning to Troy because he expects further harm from them, although Heracles' command requires him to aid their cause.

l: Troy, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Troy is the destination Philoctetes hates and refuses to approach for most of the unit. Heracles declares that Philoctetes and Neoptolemus will go there, and that Troy will fall before Philoctetes' bow.

l: Lemnos, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Lemnos has been Philoctetes' place of exile and suffering, but he finally agrees to leave it. He blesses and bids farewell to its earth, waters, shores, and surrounding landscape before beginning the voyage.

l: Philoctetes' cave, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Philoctetes' cave is his lonely shelter and the place where he has endured pain, hunger, and exile. He bids farewell to it as he prepares to leave Lemnos.

l: Achilles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Achilles is invoked as the father whose nobility Neoptolemus has inherited. Philoctetes recognizes Neoptolemus as Achilles' son, and Heracles says that Neoptolemus is necessary to Philoctetes' victory.

l: Zeus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Zeus is invoked by Philoctetes in pleas and oaths. Heracles claims to speak with authority about what Zeus intends and says that Zeus values piety above all.

l: the bow of Heracles, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Philoctetes' bow is taken from him through Neoptolemus' deceit and is treated as the essential support of his life and power. Neoptolemus returns it, and Heracles identifies it as the weapon by which Troy will be conquered.

l: Philoctetes' wound, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Philoctetes' wound causes his isolation, hunger, and inability to live among other mortals. Heracles explains that it came from approaching Chrysa's sentinel and promises that the physicians connected with Asclepius will heal it at Troy.

l: Philoctetes' exile, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Philoctetes' exile on Lemnos has lasted through severe physical and emotional suffering after the Achaeans cast him out because of his wound. He resists ending the exile by returning to Troy, but eventually agrees to leave under Heracles' command.

l: the voyage to Troy, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: The voyage to Troy is proposed by Neoptolemus and rejected by Philoctetes until Heracles commands it. At the end of the unit, Philoctetes, Neoptolemus, and the Chorus prepare to depart from Lemnos with a favorable wind.

l: healing of Philoctetes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Heracles promises that Philoctetes will first be healed of his wound at Troy. He says that Asclepius will be sent to relieve Philoctetes' pain.

l: conquest of Troy, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Heracles predicts that Philoctetes will use his bow with Neoptolemus' help to conquer Troy. He says that Philoctetes will gain unmatched renown and that Troy must fall before the Herculean bow.

l: the Trojan War, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: The Trojan War is represented through the Achaean army's efforts to bring Philoctetes to Troy and through the conflict between Troy and the Greeks. The unit establishes that Philoctetes' bow and participation are required for the Greek victory.

l: Helenus' prophecy, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: A prophecy attributed to Helenus states that Troy will fall before harvest if Philoctetes is brought to Troy and healed. Heracles confirms this outcome and presents it as part of Zeus' intention.

l: fate, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: The Chorus says that divine Destiny has bound Philoctetes in his suffering, while Neoptolemus says that mortals must bear what Heaven ordains. Heracles likewise presents Philoctetes' voyage, healing, and victory as decreed by a higher power.

l: deceit and moral right, The Seven Plays in English Verse, MONODY.
s: Neoptolemus recognizes that he acted wrongly by using deceit to take Philoctetes' bow and tries to restore what he took. The unit contrasts Odysseus' stratagem with Neoptolemus' attempt to act rightly, while also showing Philoctetes' struggle to trust an act of apparent friendship.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: Oedipus, old and blind, arrives at Colonos led by Antigone and rests near the sacred grove of the Eumenides. An Athenian warns them that the ground is forbidden, and the Chorus of Village Guardians orders Oedipus to leave after learning that he is the fate-wearied son of Laius. Oedipus argues that his crimes were committed unknowingly and that he has come under divine direction, promising blessings to those who shelter him. The Chorus agrees to let Theseus decide his fate, and Ismene arrives to join her father and sister.

l: Oedipus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: Oedipus arrives at Colonos as an aged, blind exile led by Antigone. He enters ground sacred to the Eumenides, is ordered to leave by the Chorus, and identifies himself as the son of Laius and the fate-wearied Oedipus. He maintains that his actions were unknowingly committed and that he has come on a holy mission bearing blessings for those who shelter him.

l: Antigone, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: Antigone leads her old and blind father to Colonos, finds a place for him to rest, and guides him away from the forbidden grove. She pleads with the Chorus to pity Oedipus and later recognizes Ismene approaching.

l: Ismene, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: Ismene arrives at Colonos on horseback and approaches Oedipus and Antigone. Antigone recognizes her and expects her voice to confirm her identity.

l: Creon, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: Creon is identified in the introductory account as having consented to Oedipus's banishment and as having supported the exclusion of Polynices from Thebes.

l: Theseus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: Theseus is identified as the king of Athens and the son of Aegeus. The Chorus expects him to come in person after hearing Oedipus's name and agrees that he should decide whether Oedipus may remain.

l: Chorus of Village Guardians, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: The Chorus of Village Guardians searches for Oedipus after he enters the sacred grove and orders him to leave the forbidden ground. After hearing his identity and Antigone's plea, it expresses pity but defers judgment to Theseus.

l: Thebes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: Thebes is identified in the introductory account as the place from which Oedipus was banished. The account also says that Thebes may be overcome if Oedipus dies in a foreign land.

l: Athens, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: Athens is described as the city near Colonos and as a city praised for reverence, mercy, sheltering sufferers, and comforting exiles. Oedipus appeals to Athens to protect him and not diminish its reputation through unjust treatment.

l: Colonos, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: Colonos is the place where Oedipus arrives and where the scene occurs. It is described as a sacred region near Athens, associated with Poseidon, Prometheus, and Colonos, the first of the Knights.

l: grove of the Eumenides, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: The grove of the Eumenides is a sacred and forbidden place at Colonos. Oedipus enters it unknowingly, rests near its shrine, and is directed to move to a permitted place outside it.

l: Eumenides, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: The Eumenides are described as dread sisters, children of Earth and Night, whose sanctuary is at Colonos. Oedipus addresses them as Gentle Powers and asks them to receive his prayer kindly.

l: the Gods, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: The Gods are presented as observing human righteousness and unrighteousness. Oedipus argues that reverence for the Gods requires protecting a suppliant rather than rejecting him through fear of his reputation.

l: Delphic oracle, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: The introductory account says that the Delphic oracle foretells that Thebes's enemies will prevail if Oedipus dies in a foreign land. It also says that an earlier oracle promised Oedipus rest and refuge with revered Powers, together with blessing for those who shelter him.

l: Oedipus's exile, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: Oedipus's banishment from Thebes is attributed to the command of Creon, with the consent of Oedipus's sons. The banishment leads Oedipus to wander until he reaches Colonos.

l: Oedipus's crimes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: Oedipus's crimes are identified as acts committed unknowingly. He argues that his life has endured more wrong than it has done and that his actions cannot fairly be treated as intentional guilt.

l: the blind stranger's death, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: The introductory account says that Oedipus's death in a foreign land will bring victory to the enemies of Thebes. An earlier oracle also promises that his troubled life will end after he reaches a place of refuge among revered Powers.

l: Athens's protection of Oedipus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: Athens's protection of Oedipus has not yet been granted in the dramatic action of this unit. The Chorus agrees that Theseus should decide whether Oedipus may remain, while Oedipus asks Athens to defend him as a suppliant.

l: Oedipus's promised protection of Athens, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: Oedipus says that he has come on a holy mission bearing rich blessings for the people who shelter him. The introductory account states that this blessing will be secured to Athens and denied to Thebes.

l: Oedipus's blindness, The Seven Plays in English Verse, OEDIPUS AT COLONOS
s: Oedipus is old and blind and depends on Antigone to guide him. He says that he can nevertheless 'see by sound,' and he claims that the words he speaks will be full of sight.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: Ismene visits Oedipus and reports that Eteocles and Polynices are fighting over the Theban throne, while an oracle says that Oedipus will bring salvation to the Theban race whether alive or dead. Oedipus curses his sons and refuses to aid them, praising instead Antigone and Ismene for caring for him during his exile. The Chorus instructs Oedipus in an offering to the holy powers of the grove, and Ismene goes to perform it. Oedipus also recounts that he unknowingly killed his father and fathered children with his mother, insisting that divine law frees him from guilt for the killing.

l: Oedipus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: Oedipus receives Ismene, hears of the conflict between his sons and the oracle concerning him, and declares that he will not aid Eteocles or Polynices. He praises his daughters for sustaining him in exile, accepts the Chorus's instructions for an offering, and recounts his incest and the killing of his father.

l: Ismene, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: Ismene comes to Oedipus with a trusted slave and reports the conflict between Eteocles and Polynices. She tells him that an oracle says the Theban race will seek him, alive or dead, because victory depends on him, and she goes to perform the required offering.

l: Antigone, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: Antigone has continually tended Oedipus since childhood, accompanying him through hardship, fasting, and exposure. She remains with him while Ismene performs the offering.

l: Olympian gods, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: The Gods are said to uphold Oedipus after having destroyed him, and their will is conveyed through oracles. Oedipus asks that they bring his sons' destined conflict to its appointed end.

l: the Chorus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: The Chorus expresses compassion for Oedipus and his daughters, advises him to propitiate the holy powers of the grove, and gives detailed instructions for the offering. It also questions Oedipus about his incest and the killing of his father.

l: the Cadmeans, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: The Theban race is said to seek Oedipus because the oracle declares that his presence, alive or dead, will bring it salvation. His burial near Theban land is also expected to bring it either safety or ruin depending on his wrath.

l: Thebes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: Thebè is described by Oedipus as having bound him in evil bands without his knowing the curse connected with his fate.

l: grove of the Eumenides, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: The grove received Oedipus when he first entered the land. The Chorus directs him to perform the offering beyond the grove.

l: the oracle concerning Oedipus's sons, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: The oracle says that Oedipus's sons will seek him, alive or dead, because the salvation of the Theban race and their victory depend on him. It also says that Oedipus's wrath at their tomb will bring disaster upon the brood of Cadmus.

l: the conflict between Eteocles and Polynices, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: Eteocles and Polynices first argued that the throne should remain vacant because of their father's pollution, but later turned against each other. Eteocles deprived the elder Polynices of his rule and banished him, after which Polynices secured Argive support to attack the seed of Cadmus.

l: Oedipus's exile, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: Oedipus says that when he was first suffering, the State did not grant his wish for death but later drove him permanently from his native land. His sons failed to help him, while Antigone and Ismene supported him in homeless banishment and beggary.

l: Oedipus's burial, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: Creon intends to place Oedipus near Theban land, within the reach of Theban power. His burial is considered dangerous because his wrath at the tomb could bring disaster upon the Theban side.

l: the offering to the holy powers, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: The offering requires clean water from a perennial spring, bowls wreathed with wool from a young ewe-lamb, and three libations at dawn. The last vessel is to contain water and honey, followed by eighteen olive twigs and a silent prayer to the Gentle Powers; Ismene goes to perform it.

l: parricide, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: Oedipus acknowledges that he filled his mother's bed and that his daughters are both his children and his sisters. He also admits that he killed his father, but says the killing was committed unknowingly and that divine law frees him from guilt.

l: Oedipus's two children, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: Oedipus's daughters, Antigone and Ismene, care for him when his sons do not. They support and guide him, and Ismene undertakes the offering while Antigone remains to watch over him.

l: Oedipus's sons, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: Oedipus's sons, Eteocles and Polynices, choose ambition and sovereignty over concern for their father. They fight over the Theban throne, and Oedipus refuses to help either of them, praying that their conflict end according to his wish.

l: the Theban throne, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ ISMENE.
s: Eteocles seizes the Theban throne from Polynices, who is banished and seeks Argive support to recover power. Oedipus declares that neither the reigning brother nor the exiled brother will retain or regain the throne through his aid.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Theseus welcomes Oedipus to Athens and agrees to protect him, accepting the promised benefit of Oedipus's burial place for the city. Oedipus explains that his sons seek to force him back to Thebes because a prophecy foretells their defeat by Athens, but he refuses to return and asks Theseus to let him remain. Creon arrives to take Oedipus back, then has Antigone seized and threatens to seize Oedipus as well. The Chorus of Colonian elders resists Creon's actions and calls for the ruler of Athens to intervene.

l: Theseus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Theseus recognizes Oedipus, expresses pity for him, and offers to hear and fulfill his request. He agrees to protect Oedipus, refuses to let him be taken by force, and accepts Oedipus's promised benefit to Athens.

l: Oedipus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Oedipus offers Theseus his aged body as a gift and asks to remain under Theseus's protection rather than return to Thebes. He explains that his sons now seek him because of a prophecy, condemns Creon's treatment of him, and calls upon Athens for aid when Creon attempts to seize him.

l: Antigone, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Antigone accompanies Oedipus and is seized and dragged away by Creon's attendants against her will. She cries out for help while Oedipus reaches for her but cannot prevent her removal.

l: Creon, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Creon comes from Thebes claiming that he wants to bring Oedipus back to his ancestral home. When Oedipus refuses, Creon orders Antigone taken by force and threatens to seize Oedipus, provoking resistance from the Chorus.

l: Oedipus's sons, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Oedipus's sons are said to be compelling his removal to Thebes because of the foretold consequences of his presence elsewhere. Oedipus declares that they rejected him when he wanted exile and now seek him when he refuses to return.

l: Chorus of Village Guardians, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: The Chorus praises Colonus and Athens, welcomes Oedipus's promised protection of the land, and initially supports Theseus's decision. It confronts Creon, orders him to release Antigone, and calls for the ruler of the land when Creon threatens further violence.

l: the Athenians, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: The Athenians are represented as a powerful people whose city protects Oedipus from being taken by force. Oedipus calls upon them for aid, and the Chorus asserts that Athens cannot remain a city if Creon's violence is allowed.

l: Theban citizens, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: The Thebans are said to have sent Creon to bring Oedipus back to Thebes. Creon also threatens that harming him will bring war with Thebes.

l: Athens, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Athens is portrayed as mighty, protective, and bound by friendship with Oedipus. Theseus promises that his name will shield Oedipus from injury, while Oedipus predicts that his burial in the land will benefit Athens against future enemies.

l: Thebes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Thebes is Oedipus's native land, but he refuses to return there because he believes his presence would serve its interests rather than his own. Oedipus predicts that his burial will bring destruction to Thebes's enemies, and Creon threatens war between Thebes and Athens.

l: Colonos, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Colonus is celebrated as a sacred, fertile, and divinely favored place within Athens. Oedipus seeks to remain there under Theseus's protection, and the Chorus defends the place from Creon's interference.

l: Zeus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Zeus is invoked as a witness to Oedipus's prophecy and as the divine power whose promises would make Oedipus's burial beneficial to Athens. Oedipus also invokes Zeus when praying that Creon be punished.

l: Oedipus's blindness, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Oedipus's blindness is repeatedly used by Creon to portray him as aged, helpless, and dependent on Antigone. Oedipus says that Creon, after he lost his eyes, is now taking away the people who made his darkness bearable.

l: Oedipus's exile, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Oedipus says that he was expelled from his native land by his own offspring and that return is barred to him as the man who slew his sire. He recalls that Creon once refused his request for banishment but later expelled him when Oedipus wished to remain at home.

l: the prophecy concerning Athens and Thebes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: The prophecy drives Oedipus's sons to seek his removal to Thebes because it foretells defeat by Athens in the Athenian land. Oedipus further declares that, if Zeus and Phoebus are truthful, his buried body will bring harm to his enemies and protect Athens.

l: the abduction of Antigone, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Creon orders his attendants to take Antigone by force after Oedipus refuses to return to Thebes. Antigone is dragged away against her will while the Chorus protests and demands that she be released.

l: the attempted seizure of Oedipus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: After taking Antigone, Creon announces that he will seize Oedipus and carry him away. The Chorus challenges Creon's right to do so, and Oedipus relies on the protection promised by Theseus and Athens.

l: the conflict between Athens and Thebes, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: The immediate conflict begins when Creon uses force against Oedipus and Antigone within the territory protected by Athens. Creon threatens war with Thebes if the Chorus harms him, while Oedipus predicts that future hostility between the two powers will arise and that his burial will aid Athens.

l: Oedipus's promised protection of Athens, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Oedipus promises that his burial in Athens will provide a powerful defense against its enemies. Theseus accepts this promised benefit and agrees to protect Oedipus, provided Oedipus remains under his authority and protection.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Theseus learns that Creon has seized Oedipus's two children from the sacred refuge at Colonos. He orders the people of Athens to pursue the captors and demands that Creon lead him to the abducted maidens. Creon claims that Athens would not willingly shelter Oedipus, whom he calls an incestuous parricide, while Oedipus argues that his crimes were committed unknowingly. Theseus rejects Creon's actions as unlawful and vows to restore the children to Oedipus.

l: Theseus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Theseus is told that Creon has taken Oedipus's two children and orders horsemen and footmen to pursue them. He condemns Creon's seizure of suppliants from Colonos and insists that Creon lead him to the children, accompanying him as an escort. Theseus vows not to rest until he restores the children to Oedipus.

l: Oedipus, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Oedipus tells Theseus that Creon has wronged him by taking the two children who mean everything to him. He defends himself against Creon's accusations, arguing that he killed his father and married his mother without knowing their identities. He appeals to the gods who protect the hallowed realm to support him against Creon's violence.

l: Creon, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Creon admits that he seized Oedipus's children and claims he acted because he believed Athens would not harbor Oedipus, whom he calls an incestuous parricide. He says that Oedipus's curses against him and his family moved him to retaliate. After Theseus challenges him, Creon is compelled to lead the way toward the children.

l: Oedipus's two children, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Oedipus's two children have been captured and carried away by Creon. Theseus orders a pursuit to rescue them and demands that Creon bring them into his presence.

l: Athens, The Seven Plays in English Verse, _Enter_ THESEUS.
s: Athens is described as a city that observes justice and equity, respects the gods, and does not ratify actions apart from law. Theseus declares that Athens must not appear weaker than one man and acts to defend its laws and honor.
